topics.title: na_values declares the sentinels
topics.body: A CSV often encodes missing data as "NA", "-" or "999". `na_values` names them at load time, so they arrive as NaN instead of as a category or a number.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "v\n10\nNA"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), na_values=["NA"])
print(df["v"].isna().tolist())

topics.title: nrows reads a sample of a big file
topics.body: `nrows` reads the first n data rows, which is enough to check the columns and dtypes of a file that would take minutes to parse fully.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "a,b\n1,2\n3,4\n5,6"
print(pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), nrows=1).shape)

topics.title: to_json orient chooses the shape
topics.body: `orient="records"` writes one object per row, which is what an API expects. The default is column-oriented and reads very differently.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [2]})
print(df.to_json(orient="records"))

topics.title: index_col moves a column into the index at load
topics.body: `index_col` avoids a later `set_index`, and it keeps the column out of the data from the start, which is why an id often belongs there.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

print(pd.read_csv(StringIO("id,v\n1,10\n"), index_col="id").index.tolist())

interview.q: How do you make a CSV load reproducible?
interview.answer: Pin the contract: `sep`, `dtype`, `parse_dates`, `na_values`, `usecols`. Then the same file produces the same frame on every machine, and a change in the source fails at the boundary instead of in a later mean.

interview.q: Why is a Parquet export often preferred to CSV for downstream analysis?
interview.answer: Parquet stores the schema and the types, reads only the columns requested, and is far faster to parse at size. CSV is portable and human-readable, which is the reason it is still the interchange default.

topics.title: suffixes name the collision
topics.body: When both sides have a column of the same name, `suffixes` decides the two new names. Naming them explicitly keeps a report readable.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "v": [10]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "v": [20]})
out = a.merge(b, on="id", suffixes=("_left", "_right"))
print(out.columns.tolist())

topics.title: concat stacks columns with axis=1
topics.body: `axis=1` places frames side by side and aligns them by index. Misaligned labels produce NaN rows, which is the sign the indexes did not agree.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"y": [2]})
print(pd.concat([a, b], axis=1).shape)

topics.title: merge on the index needs no key column
topics.body: With `left_index` and `right_index` the join uses labels, which is how two tables already indexed by the same key are combined without a reset.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1]}, index=["k"])
b = pd.DataFrame({"y": [2]}, index=["k"])
print(a.merge(b, left_index=True, right_index=True).values.tolist())

topics.title: indicator turns a mystery into a filter
topics.body: `_merge` labels each row as `both`, `left_only` or `right_only`. Filtering `left_only` is the "who never matched" report.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [2]})
out = a.merge(b, on="id", how="left", indicator=True)
print(out["_merge"].tolist())

interview.q: How do you prove a join did not change the grain?
interview.answer: Record the row count and the key's uniqueness on both sides, then compare the result with the expected relationship: one-to-one keeps the count, one-to-many multiplies it by the matches. `validate` turns the expectation into an assertion.

interview.q: What is the risk of `how="outer"` on a large table?
interview.answer: It keeps unmatched keys from both sides, so the result grows and the NaN columns mix two different kinds of missingness — a genuinely absent record and a record that exists but has no value. Report the counts of each separately.

topics.title: as_index=False keeps the key as a column
topics.body: By default the group key becomes the index. `as_index=False` keeps it as a column, which is what a flat export or a chart expects.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune"], "v": [1, 2]})
out = df.groupby("city", as_index=False)["v"].sum()
print(out.columns.tolist())

topics.title: dropna=False keeps the missing key
topics.body: Rows with a missing group key are dropped by default, so the totals shrink. Keeping them shows that the key itself is incomplete.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", None], "v": [1, 2]})
print(len(df.groupby("city")["v"].sum()))
print(len(df.groupby("city", dropna=False)["v"].sum()))

topics.title: ngroup numbers the groups
topics.body: `ngroup()` returns a group number per row, which is how a categorical segment becomes a compact integer feature for a model.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["b", "a", "b"]})
print(df.groupby("city").ngroup().tolist())

topics.title: size counts rows, count counts values
topics.body: `size` includes missing values, `count` does not. On a sparse column the two answers differ, and the wrong one overstates the evidence.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a"], "v": [1.0, None]})
out = df.groupby("g").agg(n=("v", "size"), filled=("v", "count"))
print(out.values.tolist())

interview.q: Why report a group size beside a group mean?
interview.answer: A mean over one or two rows has no meaningful spread and cannot be compared with a mean over thousands. The size column lets the reader see which conclusions are supported and which are anecdote.

interview.q: What is the difference between `agg` and `transform` in one example?
interview.answer: `agg("mean")` collapses each city to a single row — a report. `transform("mean")` returns the city mean on every original row, so it can be compared with the row's own value to find above-average records.

topics.title: margins adds the totals row
topics.body: `margins=True` appends an All row and column, so a pivot table carries its own totals instead of a second computation.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "v": [1, 2, 3]})
t = df.pivot_table(index="city", columns="year", values="v", aggfunc="sum", margins=True, fill_value=0)
print(t.index.tolist())

topics.title: stack and unstack are inverses
topics.body: `stack` moves the innermost column level into the index; `unstack` moves it back. A round trip is a good way to prove a reshape lost nothing.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [2]}, index=["r"])
long = df.stack()
print(long.tolist())
print(long.unstack().values.tolist())

topics.title: wide_to_long needs a stub name
topics.body: `wide_to_long` collects columns that share a prefix, so `sale_2025`, `sale_2026` become one value column with the year kept in a new column.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "sale_2025": [10], "sale_2026": [20]})
long = pd.wide_to_long(df, stubnames="sale", i="id", j="year", sep="_")
print(long["sale"].tolist())

topics.title: crosstab can show shares
topics.body: `normalize="columns"` divides each column by its total, so a crosstab reports a share rather than a count — the difference between 200 rows and 20%.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": ["x", "x", "y"], "b": [1, 1, 0]})
print(pd.crosstab(df["a"], df["b"], normalize="columns").round(2).values.tolist())

interview.answer: One row per observation, one column per variable, one value per cell. Wide monthly columns violate it because the month is a variable spread across headers; melting restores the rule and makes grouping and plotting direct.

interview.q: Why does a pivot show NaN where you expect zero?
interview.answer: The combination does not exist in the data, so there is no group to aggregate. `fill_value=0` states the business meaning — no activity — instead of leaving the reader to guess between absent and unknown.

topics.title: strftime formats a datetime column
topics.body: `.dt.strftime` turns timestamps into the exact text a report needs, and it is the safest way to compare a month label across two sources.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(["2026-01-05"]))
print(s.dt.strftime("%b %Y").tolist())

topics.title: DateOffset moves by calendar units
topics.body: `pd.DateOffset(months=1)` respects month lengths, unlike adding 30 days. It is the correct arithmetic for billing cycles and renewals.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

start = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-31")
print((start + pd.DateOffset(months=1)).strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))

topics.title: Localise, then convert
topics.body: `tz_localize` attaches a timezone to naive timestamps; `tz_convert` moves an aware series to another zone. Calling convert first is the classic error.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01 00:00"]))
aware = s.dt.tz_localize("Asia/Kolkata").dt.tz_convert("UTC")
print(aware.dt.hour.tolist())

topics.title: asfreq shows the empty periods
topics.body: `asfreq` reindexes to a frequency and leaves NaN where no observation exists, which exposes gaps that a resample sum would turn into zero.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1.0, 3.0], index=pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-01-03"]))
print(s.asfreq("D").isna().sum())

interview.q: Why does resample produce months that a groupby would miss?
interview.answer: Resample generates the calendar for the range, including empty periods, so a gap is visible as a row. Grouping on an extracted month only returns the months that have data, which hides the gap.

interview.q: What does a rolling window assume about the data?
interview.answer: That the index is evenly spaced and ordered, and that the window's rows are comparable periods. On uneven sampling or duplicate timestamps the window mixes different amounts of time, so the mean is not comparable across rows.
